Sapeva bene cosa aveva ereditato da lei: la sua [[Beauty|bellezza]] e la sua passione per la bellezza altrui. Lei rideva di lui, indossando quel vestito sciolto da bacchantessa; i suoi capelli erano adornati di foglie di vite. Il colore viola si riversava dalla coppa che teneva in mano. I garofani del dipinto erano appassiti, ma quegli occhi rimanevano meravigliosi per la loro profondità e il loro splendore cromatico. Sembravano seguirlo ovunque andasse.
Eppure qualcuno aveva antenati nella letteratura tanto quanto nella propria razza; forse molti di loro erano più simili a lui per tipo e temperamento, e certamente esercitavano su di lui un’influenza di cui era pienamente consapevole. C’erano momenti in cui a [[Dorian Gray]] sembrava che tutta la [[history|storia]] non fosse altro che il racconto della sua stessa vita, non così come l’aveva vissuta realmente, ma così come la sua [[Imagination|immaginazione]] l’aveva creata per lui, così com’era nella sua mente e nelle sue passioni. Gli pareva di aver conosciuto tutti quegli strani, terribili personaggi che erano apparsi sulla scena del mondo, rendendo il peccato così meraviglioso e il male così pieno di sottigliezze. Gli sembrava che, in qualche modo misterioso, le loro vite fossero state anche sue.  
Il [[Hero|eroe]] di quel meraviglioso [[Novel|romanzo]] che aveva avuto un tale influenza sulla sua vita aveva conosciuto anch’egli questa strana fantasia. Nel settimo capitolo racconta come, incoronato di alloro per evitare che lo colpisse la [[Lightning|fulmine]], si fosse seduto, come Tiberio, in un [[Garden|giardino]] a Capri, leggendo quei libri vergognosi di Elephantis, mentre nani e pavoni camminavano intorno a lui e il suonatore di flauto derideva colui che agitava l’incensiere; come Caligola si fosse divertito con i fantini in abiti verdi nelle loro stalle e avesse cenato in un mangiatore d’avorio insieme a un [[Horse|cavallo]] con la fronte adornata di gemme; come Domiziano si fosse aggirato in un corridoio rivestito di specchi di marmo, cercando con occhi stanchi il riflesso del pugnale che avrebbe posto fine alla sua vita, e avesse sofferto di quell’ennui, di quella terribile noia della vita che colpisce coloro a cui essa non nega nulla; come avesse guardato attraverso uno specchio di smeraldo i disordini del circo. E poi, su un palanchino fatto di perle e porpora, trainato da muli con zoccoli d’argento, fosse stato portato lungo la Via dei Granati fino a una [[house|casa]] d’oro, dove aveva sentito le persone piangere per Nerone Cesare mentre passava. E come Elagabalo si fosse dipinto il viso con colori, avesse partecipato alle danze tra le donne, avesse portato la [[Moon|luna]] da Cartagine e l’avesse data in un matrimonio mistico al Sole.
Ancora e ancora Dorian leggeva questo fantastico capitolo, nonché i due capitoli che seguivano immediatamente; in essi, come in alcuni curiosi arazzi o abilmente realizzati smalti, erano raffigurate le forme orribili e al contempo belle di coloro che vizio, [[Blood|sangue]] e stanchezza avevano reso mostri o pazzi: Filippo, [[Duke of Milan|Duca di Milano]], che uccise sua moglie e le dipinse le labbra con un rosso [[Poison|)veleno]] affinché il suo [[Lover|amante]] potesse succhiare la [[Death|morte]] da quel cadavere che accarezzava; Pietro Barbi, il veneziano noto come Paolo II, che nella sua [[Vanity|vanezza]] cercò di assumersi il titolo di Formosus, e la cui tiara, valutata duecentomila fiorini, fu comprata al prezzo di un terribile peccato; Gian Maria Visconti, che usava cani per inseguire uomini vivi e il cui corpo assassinato fu coperto di rose da una prostituta che lo aveva amato; i Borgia, con Fratricide a cavallo accanto a loro e il mantello macchiato dal [[Blood|sangue]] di Perotto; Pietro Riario, giovane Cardinale Arcivescovo di Firenze, [[Child|bambino]] e servitore di Sisto IV, la cui [[Beauty|bellezza]] era eguagliata solo dalla sua dissolutezza; che ricevette Leonora d’Aragona in un padiglione fatto di seta bianca e cremisi, pieno di ninfe e centauri, e che incastonò un ragazzo affinché potesse servirlo alla festa come Ganymede o Hylas; Ezzelin, la cui [[Melancholy|melanconia]] poteva essere curata solo dallo spettacolo della [[Death|morte]], e che aveva una passione per il rosso [[Blood|sangue]], come altri uomini ne hanno per il vino rosso; figlio del Diavolo, si diceva, e colui che aveva tradito suo padre giocando a dadi per ottenere la propria [[Soul|'anima]]; Giambattista Cibo, che in segno di scherno prese il nome di [[Innocent|Innocente]] e nel cui corpo intorpidito un medico ebreo infuse il [[Blood|sangue]] di tre ragazzi; Sigismondo Malatesta, l’[[Lover|amante]] di Isotta e signore di Rimini, la cui effigie fu bruciata a Roma come nemica di Dio e degli uomini; che strangolò Polyssena con un fazzoletto, diede [[Poison|)veleno]] a Ginevra d’Este in una coppa di smeraldo, e per onorare una vergognosa passione costruì una chiesa pagana per il culto cristiano; Carlo VI, che amava così follemente la moglie di suo fratello da essere avvertito da un lebbroso dell’insanità che lo stava colpendo; e, con il suo giubbotto tagliato alla moda, il cappello incastonato di gioielli e i riccioli simili ad acanti, Grifonetto Baglioni, che uccise Astorre insieme a sua moglie e Simonetto insieme al suo paggio; la cui bellezza era tale che, mentre giaceva morente nella piazza gialla di Perugia, coloro che lo odiavano non poterono fare a meno di piangere; e Atalanta, che lo aveva maledetto, ma poi lo benedisse.
C'era una terribile fascinazione in tutto ciò. Li vedeva di [[Night|notte]], e durante il giorno essi turbavano la sua [[Imagination|immaginazione]]. La [[Renaissance|Rinascita]] conosceva strani metodi di avvelenamento: avvelenamento tramite un elmo e una torcia accesa, tramite un guanto ricamato e un ventaglio incastonato di gemme, tramite un pomander dorato e una catena d'ambra. [[Dorian Gray]] era stato avvelenato da un libro. C'erano momenti in cui considerava il male semplicemente come un mezzo per realizzare la sua concezione della bellezza.

CHAPTER 12
It was on the ninth of November, the eve of his own thirty-eighth birthday, as he often remembered afterwards.
He was walking [[Home|home]] about eleven o’[[Clock|clock]] from Lord Henry’s, where he had been dining, and was wrapped in heavy furs, as the [[Night|night]] was cold and foggy. At the corner of Grosvenor Square and South Audley Street, a man passed him in the mist, walking very fast and with the collar of his grey ulster turned up. He had a bag in his hand. Dorian recognized him. It was [[Basil Hallward]]. A strange sense of [[Fear|fear]], for which he could not account, came over him. He made no sign of recognition and went on quickly in the direction of his own [[house]].
But Hallward had seen him. Dorian heard him first stopping on the pavement and then hurrying after him. In a few moments, his hand was on his arm.
“Dorian! What an extraordinary piece of luck! I have been waiting for you in your library ever since nine o’[[Clock|clock]]. Finally I took pity on your tired servant and told him to go to bed, as he let me out. I am off to [[Paris]] by the midnight train, and I particularly wanted to see you before I left. I thought it was you, or rather your fur coat, as you passed me. But I wasn’t quite sure. Didn’t you recognize me?”
“In this fog, my dear Basil? Why, I can’t even recognize Grosvenor Square. I believe my [[house]] is somewhere about here, but I don’t feel at all certain about it. I am sorry you are going away, as I have not seen you for ages. But I suppose you will be back soon?”
“No: I am going to be out of England for six months. I intend to take a studio in [[Paris]] and shut myself up till I have finished a great picture I have in my head. However, it wasn’t about myself I wanted to talk. Here we are at your door. Let me come in for a moment. I have something to say to you.”
“I shall be charmed. But won’t you miss your train?” said [[Dorian Gray]] languidly as he passed up the steps and opened the door with his latch-key.
The lamplight struggled out through the fog, and Hallward looked at his watch. “I have heaps of [[Time|time]],” he answered. “The train doesn’t go till twelve-fifteen, and it is only just eleven. In fact, I was on my way to the club to look for you, when I met you. You see, I shan’t have any delay about luggage, as I have sent on my heavy things. All I have with me is in this bag, and I can easily get to Victoria in twenty minutes.”
Dorian looked at him and smiled. “What a way for a fashionable painter to travel! A Gladstone bag and an ulster! Come in, or the fog will get into the [[house]]. And mind you don’t talk about anything serious. Nothing is serious nowadays. At least nothing should be.”
Hallward shook his head, as he entered, and followed Dorian into the library. There was a bright wood [[Fire|fire]] blazing in the large open hearth. The lamps were lit, and an open Dutch silver spirit-case stood, with some siphons of soda-[[Water|water]] and large cut-glass tumblers, on a little marqueterie table.
“You see your servant made me quite at [[Home|home]], Dorian. He gave me everything I wanted, including your best gold-tipped cigarettes. He is a most hospitable creature. I like him much better than the Frenchman you used to have. What has become of the Frenchman, by the bye?”
Dorian shrugged his shoulders. “I believe he married Lady Radley’s maid, and has established her in [[Paris]] as an English dressmaker. Anglomania is very fashionable over there now, I hear. It seems silly of the French, doesn’t it? But — do you know? — he was not at all a bad servant. I never liked him, but I had nothing to complain about. One often imagines things that are quite absurd. He was really very devoted to me and seemed quite sorry when he went away. Have another brandy-and-soda? Or would you like hock-and-seltzer? I always take hock-and-seltzer myself. There is sure to be some in the next room.”
“Thanks, I won’t have anything more,” said the painter, taking his cap and coat off and throwing them on the bag that he had placed in the corner. “And now, my dear fellow, I want to speak to you seriously. Don’t frown like that. You make it so much more difficult for me.”
“What is it all about?” cried Dorian in his petulant way, flinging himself down on the sofa. “I [[Hope|hope]] it is not about myself. I am tired of myself to-[[Night|night]]. I should like to be somebody else.”
“It is about yourself,” answered Hallward in his [[Grave|grave]] deep voice, “and I must say it to you. I shall only keep you half an hour.”
Dorian sighed and lit a cigarette. “Half an hour!” he murmured.
“It is not much to ask of you, Dorian, and it is entirely for your own sake that I am speaking. I think it right that you should know that the most dreadful things are being said against you in [[London]].”
“I don’t wish to know anything about them. I [[Love|love]] scandals about other people, but scandals about myself don’t interest me. They have not got the charm of novelty.”
“They must interest you, Dorian. Every gentleman is interested in his good name. You don’t want people to talk of you as something vile and degraded. Of course, you have your position, and your wealth, and all that kind of thing. But position and wealth are not everything. Mind you, I don’t believe these rumours at all. At least, I can’t believe them when I see you. Sin is a thing that writes itself across a man’s face. It cannot be concealed. People talk sometimes of secret vices. There are no such things. If a wretched man has a vice, it shows itself in the lines of his mouth, the droop of his eyelids, the moulding of his hands even. Somebody — I won’t mention his name, but you know him — came to me last year to have his portrait done. I had never seen him before, and had never heard anything about him at the [[Time|time]], though I have heard a good deal since. He offered an extravagant price. I refused him. There was something in the shape of his fingers that I hated. I know now that I was quite right in what I fancied about him. His life is dreadful. But you, Dorian, with your pure, bright, [[Innocent|innocent]] face, and your marvellous untroubled youth — I can’t believe anything against you. And yet I see you very seldom, and you never come down to the studio now, and when I am away from you, and I hear all these hideous things that people are whispering about you, I don’t know what to say. Why is it, Dorian, that a man like the Duke of Berwick [[Leaves|leaves]] the room of a club when you enter it? Why is it that so many gentlemen in [[London]] will neither go to your [[house]] or invite you to theirs? You used to be a friend of Lord Staveley. I met him at dinner last week. Your name happened to come up in conversation, in connection with the miniatures you have lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said that you might have the most artistic tastes, but that you were a man whom no pure-minded girl should be allowed to know, and whom no chaste woman should sit in the same room with. I reminded him that I was a friend of yours, and asked him what he meant. He told me. He told me right out before everybody. It was horrible! Why is your [[Friendship|friendship]] so fatal to young men? There was that wretched boy in the Guards who committed [[suicide]]. You were his great friend. There was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with a tarnished name. You and he were inseparable. What about Adrian Singleton and his dreadful end? What about Lord [[Kent]]’s only son and his career? I met his father yesterday in St. James’s Street. He seemed broken with shame and sorrow. What about the young Duke of Perth? What sort of life has he got now? What gentleman would associate with him?”
“Stop, Basil. You are talking about things of which you know nothing,” said [[Dorian Gray]], biting his lip, and with a note of infinite contempt in his voice. “You ask me why Berwick [[Leaves|leaves]] a room when I enter it. It is because I know everything about his life, not because he knows anything about mine. With such [[Blood|blood]] as he has in his veins, how could his record be clean? You ask me about Henry Ashton and young Perth. Did I teach the one his vices, and the other his debauchery? If [[Kent]]’s silly son takes his wife from the streets, what is that to me? If Adrian Singleton writes his friend’s name across a bill, am I his keeper? I know how people chatter in England. The middle classes air their moral prejudices over their gross dinner-tables, and whisper about what they call the profligacies of their betters in order to try and pretend that they are in smart society and on intimate terms with the people they slander. In this country, it is enough for a man to have distinction and brains for every common tongue to wag against him. And what sort of lives do these people, who pose as being moral, lead themselves? My dear fellow, you forget that we are in the native land of the hypocrite.”
“Dorian,” cried Hallward, “that is not the question. England is bad enough I know, and English society is all wrong. That is the reason why I want you to be fine. You have not been fine. One has a right to judge of a man by the effect he has over his friends. Yours seem to lose all sense of [[Honour|honour]], of goodness, of purity. You have filled them with a [[Madness|madness]] for pleasure. They have gone down into the depths. You led them there. Yes: you led them there, and yet you can smile, as you are smiling now. And there is worse behind. I know you and Harry are inseparable. Surely for that reason, if for none other, you should not have made his sister’s name a by-word.”
“Take care, Basil. You go too far.”
“I must speak, and you must listen. You shall listen. When you met Lady Gwendolen, not a breath of scandal had ever touched her. Is there a single decent woman in [[London]] now who would drive with her in the park? Why, even her children are not allowed to live with her. Then there are other stories — stories that you have been seen creeping at [[Dawn|dawn]] out of dreadful houses and slinking in disguise into the foulest dens in [[London]]. Are they true? Can they be true? When I first heard them, I laughed. I hear them now, and they make me shudder. What about your country-[[house]] and the life that is led there? Dorian, you don’t know what is said about you. I won’t tell you that I don’t want to preach to you. I remember Harry saying once that every man who turned himself into an amateur curate for the moment always began by saying that, and then proceeded to break his word. I do want to preach to you. I want you to lead such a life as will make the world respect you. I want you to have a clean name and a fair record. I want you to get rid of the dreadful people you associate with. Don’t shrug your shoulders like that. Don’t be so indifferent. You have a wonderful influence. Let it be for good, not for evil. They say that you corrupt every one with whom you become intimate, and that it is quite sufficient for you to enter a [[house]] for shame of some kind to follow after. I don’t know whether it is so or not. How should I know? But it is said of you. I am told things that it seems impossible to [[Doubt|doubt]]. Lord [[Gloucester]] was one of my greatest friends at [[Oxford]]. He showed me a letter that his wife had written to him when she was dying [[Alone|alone]] in her villa at Mentone. Your name was implicated in the most terrible confession I ever read. I told him that it was absurd — that I knew you thoroughly and that you were incapable of anything of the kind. Know you? I [[Wonder|wonder]] do I know you? Before I could answer that, I should have to see your [[Soul|soul]].”
“To see my [[Soul|soul]]!” muttered [[Dorian Gray]], starting up from the sofa and turning almost white from [[Fear|fear]].
“Yes,” answered Hallward gravely, and with deep-toned sorrow in his voice, “to see your [[Soul|soul]]. But only God can do that.”
A bitter laugh of mockery broke from the lips of the younger man. “You shall see it yourself, to-[[Night|night]]!” he cried, seizing a lamp from the table. “Come: it is your own handiwork. Why shouldn’t you look at it? You can tell the world all about it afterwards, if you choose. Nobody would believe you. If they did believe you, they would like me all the better for it. I know the age better than you do, though you will prate about it so tediously. Come, I tell you. You have chattered enough about corruption. Now you shall look on it face to face.”
There was the [[Madness|madness]] of [[Pride|pride]] in every word he uttered. He stamped his foot upon the ground in his boyish insolent manner. He felt a terrible joy at the thought that some one else was to share his secret, and that the man who had painted the portrait that was the origin of all his shame was to be burdened for the rest of his life with the hideous [[Memory|memory]] of what he had done.
“Yes,” he continued, coming closer to him and looking steadfastly into his stern eyes, “I shall show you my [[Soul|soul]]. You shall see the thing that you fancy only God can see.”
Hallward started back. “This is blasphemy, Dorian!” he cried. “You must not say things like that. They are horrible, and they don’t mean anything.”
“You think so?” He laughed again.
“I know so. As for what I said to you to-[[Night|night]], I said it for your good. You know I have been always a stanch friend to you.”
“Don’t touch me. Finish what you have to say.”
A twisted flash of [[Pain|pain]] shot across the painter’s face. He paused for a moment, and a wild feeling of pity came over him. After all, what right had he to pry into the life of [[Dorian Gray]]? If he had done a tithe of what was rumoured about him, how much he must have suffered! Then he straightened himself up, and walked over to the [[Fire|fire]]-place, and stood there, looking at the burning logs with their frostlike ashes and their throbbing cores of flame.
“I am waiting, Basil,” said the young man in a hard clear voice.
He turned round. “What I have to say is this,” he cried. “You must give me some answer to these horrible charges that are made against you. If you tell me that they are absolutely untrue from beginning to end, I shall believe you. Deny them, Dorian, deny them! Can’t you see what I am going through? My God! don’t tell me that you are bad, and corrupt, and shameful.”
[[Dorian Gray]] smiled. There was a curl of contempt in his lips. “Come upstairs, Basil,” he said quietly. “I keep a diary of my life from day to day, and it never [[Leaves|leaves]] the room in which it is written. I shall show it to you if you come with me.”
“I shall come with you, Dorian, if you wish it. I see I have missed my train. That makes no matter. I can go to-morrow. But don’t ask me to read anything to-[[Night|night]]. All I want is a plain answer to my question.”
“That shall be given to you upstairs. I could not give it here. You will not have to read long.”

**CAPITOLO 12**  
Era il nove novembre, la vigilia del suo trentottesimo compleanno, come ricordava spesso in seguito.  
Stava tornando a casa intorno alle undici di sera da Lord Henry’s, dove aveva cenato, avvolto in pesanti pellicce: la notte era fredda e nebbiosa. All’angolo tra Grosvenor Square e South Audley Street, un uomo gli passò accanto nella nebbia, camminando molto velocemente con il colletto del suo ulster grigio rialzato; aveva una borsa in mano. Dorian lo riconobbe: era **Basil Hallward**. Gli venne un strano senso di **paura**, che non riusciva a spiegarsi. Non fece alcun segno di riconoscimento e proseguì rapidamente verso la sua casa.  
Ma Hallward lo aveva visto. Dorian sentì che si fermava sul marciapiede, poi lo inseguiva di corsa. In pochi istanti, l’uomo gli afferrò il braccio.  
“Dorian! Che strana coincidenza. Sono stato ad aspettarti nella tua biblioteca fin dalle nove. Alla fine ho avuto pietà del tuo servitore stanco e gli ho detto di andare a letto; poi sono venuto da te. Parto per **Parigi** con il treno di mezzanotte e volevo assolutamente vederti prima di partire. Pensavo fossi tu, o meglio, il tuo cappotto di pelliccia. Ma non ne ero del tutto sicuro. Non mi hai riconosciuto?”  
“Con questa nebbia, caro Basil? Non riesco nemmeno a riconoscere Grosvenor Square. Credo che la mia casa sia da queste parti, ma non ne sono certo. Mi dispiace che tu vada via. Non ti vedo da tanto tempo. Ma immagino tornerai presto, vero?”  
“No. Sarò via dall’Inghilterra per sei mesi. Intendo prendere uno studio a **Parigi** e dedicarmi completamente a un grande dipinto che ho in mente. Comunque, non era di me che volevo parlare. Ecco, siamo arrivati alla tua porta. Lasciami entrare un attimo. Ho qualcosa da dirti.”  
“Ne sarò felice. Ma non perderai il treno?” disse **Dorian Gray** con aria languida, mentre saliva i gradini e apriva la porta con la chiave.  
La luce della lampada si fece strada nella nebbia; Hallward guardò l’orologio. “Ho un sacco di tempo,” rispose. “Il treno parte solo alle dodici e mezza. Sono appena le undici. In realtà stavo andando al club per cercarti, quando ti ho incontrato. Non avrò problemi con i bagagli: ho già spedito le cose pesanti. Tutto quello che ho con me è in questa borsa. Posso arrivare alla stazione di Victoria in venti minuti.”  
Dorian lo guardò e sorrise. “Che modo strano per un pittore alla moda di viaggiare. Una borsa di Gladstone e un ulster. Entra. Altrimenti la nebbia entrerà in casa. E stai attento a non parlare di cose serie. Oggi giorno non c’è nulla di serio. Almeno, non dovrebbe esserci.”
Hallward scosse la testa entrando e seguì Dorian nella biblioteca. Nel grande camino aperto ardeva un fuoco di legna vivace; le lampade erano accese, e su un piccolo tavolo intarsiato c’era una scatola d’argento olandese con alcuni sifoni contenenti soda acquosa e grandi bicchieri di vetro tagliato.  
“Vedi come il tuo servitore mi ha reso davvero a mio agio, Dorian. Mi ha fornito tutto ciò che desideravo, comprese le tue migliori sigarette con la punta d’oro. È davvero una persona molto ospitale. Mi piace molto di più di quel francese che avevi prima. Che fine ha fatto, a proposito?”  
Dorian alzò le spalle. “Credo che abbia sposato la cameriera di Lady Radley e l’abbia stabilita a Parigi come sarta inglese. Dicono che l’anglofilia sia molto in voga laggiù, ora. Sembra stupido da parte dei francesi, non trovi? Ma, sai una cosa? Non era affatto un cattivo servitore. Non mi piaceva, ma non avevo nulla di cui lamentarmi. Spesso si immaginano cose assurde. Era davvero molto devoto a me e sembrava molto dispiaciuto quando se n’è andato. Ne vuoi un altro bicchiere di brandy con soda? O preferisci l’hock-and-seltzer? Io lo prendo sempre. Sicuramente ne avremo in quella stanza accanto.”  
“Grazie, non ne voglio più,” disse il pittore, togliendosi cappello e cappotto e gettandoli sulla borsa che aveva posizionato nell’angolo. “Ora, caro amico, devo parlarti seriamente. Non fare quella faccia scura. Mi rendi le cose molto più difficili, ”  
“Di cosa si tratta?” chiese Dorian in tono petulante, lasciandosi cadere sul divano. “Spero che non sia niente che riguarda me. Sono stanco di me stesso. Vorrei essere qualcun altro, ”  
“Si tratta proprio di te,” rispose Hallward con voce grave. “Devo dirtelo. Ti terrò qui solo mezz’ora.”  
Dorian sospirò e accese una sigaretta. “Mezz’ora, ” mormorò.  
“Non è molto chiedere, Dorian. E lo faccio esclusivamente per il tuo bene. Penso sia giusto che tu sappia che in Londra si stanno dicendo le cose più terribili su di te, ”  
“Non voglio saperne nulla. Mi piacciono gli scandali altrui, ma quelli che riguardano me non m’interessano affatto. Non hanno il fascino della novità, ”
“Dovrebbero interessarti, Dorian. Ogni gentiluomo tiene molto alla propria reputazione. Non vorrai certo che la gente parli di te in termini disonorevoli, vero? Certo, hai una posizione sociale elevata e ricchezza. Ma queste cose non sono tutto. A dire il vero, non credo affatto a queste voci. Almeno, non riesco a crederci quando ti vedo: il peccato si legge chiaramente sul volto di un uomo; non può essere nascosto. A volte la gente parla di vizi segreti. Ma non esistono cose del genere. Se un uomo ha un vizio, questo si riflette nei tratti del suo viso, nel modo in cui tiene le mani. Qualcuno. Non dirò il nome, è venuto da me l’anno scorso per farsi ritrarre. Non lo avevo mai visto prima, e all’epoca non sapevo nulla di lui. Ma da allora ho sentito molte cose su di lui. Mi ha offerto una somma enorme. L’ho rifiutata: c’era qualcosa nei suoi lineamenti che mi ripugnava. Ora so di aver avuto ragione. La sua vita è orribile. Ma tu, Dorian, con il tuo viso puro, innocente, la tua giovinezza serena e incantevole. Non riesco a credere a nulla contro di te. Eppure ti vedo molto raramente. Ormai non vieni più nello studio. Quando non sei con me, ascolto tutte queste orribili voci che la gente mormora su di te. Non so cosa pensare. Perché mai un uomo come il Duca di Berwick lascia la sala di un club non appena entri tu? Perché tanti gentiluomini di Londra né vanno a casa tua né ti invitano nelle loro case? Un tempo eri amico di Lord Staveley. L’ho incontrato a cena la scorsa settimana: il tuo nome è stato menzionato in relazione alle miniature che hai prestato all’esposizione del Dudley. Staveley ha detto che forse hai gusti artistici raffinati, ma che non sei un uomo con cui una ragazza onesta dovrebbe avere a che fare. Gli ho ricordato che sono tuo amico e gli ho chiesto cosa intendesse. Me lo ha detto apertamente, davanti a tutti. È stato orribile. Perché la tua “amicizia” è così pericolosa per i giovani uomini? C’è stato quel povero ragazzo delle Guardie che si è suicidato. Eri suo grande amico. C’è stato Sir Henry Ashton, che ha dovuto lasciare l’Inghilterra con una reputazione macchiata. Tu e lui eravate inseparabili. E poi Adrian Singleton. E la sua terribile fine. E il figlio unico di Lord Kent. Che vita ha ora? Quale gentiluomo vorrebbe frequentarlo?”
“Fermati, Basil. Stai parlando di cose di cui non sai nulla,” disse [[Dorian Gray]], mordendosi il labbro e con un tono di infinito disprezzo nella voce. “Mi chiedi perché Berwick lascia una stanza non appena entro io. È perché so tutto della sua vita, non perché lui sappia qualcosa della mia. Con quel tipo di [[Blood|sangue]] che scorre nelle sue vene, come potrebbe la sua reputazione essere pulita? Mi chiedi di Henry Ashton e del giovane Perth. Ho forse insegnato al primo i suoi vizi e al secondo le sue dissolutezze? Se il figlio sciocco di [[Kent]] prende una donna dalle strade, che cosa c’entro io con questo? Se Adrian Singleton scrive il nome del suo amico su un conto bancario, sono forse io il responsabile? So bene come la gente in Inghilterra chiacchiera. Le classi medie esprimono i loro pregiudizi morali a tavola, sussurrando delle presunte dissolutezze delle persone più nobili, nel tentativo di far credere di appartenere a una società raffinata e di avere rapporti intimi con coloro che diffamano. In questo paese, basta che un uomo abbia distinzione e intelligenza perché tutti inizino a parlare male di lui. E poi, che tipo di vita conducono queste persone che si fanno passare per morali? Caro mio, dimentichi che ci troviamo nel paese natale dell’ipocrita, ”  
“Dorian,” esclamò Hallward, “non è questo il punto. So bene che l’Inghilterra sia un posto orribile, e che la società inglese sia completamente sbagliata. È proprio per questo che voglio che tu diventi migliore. Non lo sei stato. Si ha il diritto di giudicare una persona in base all’influenza che esercita sui propri amici. I tuoi amici sembrano aver perso ogni senso di [[Honour|onore]], di bontà, di purezza. Hai infuso in loro una follia per il piacere. Li hai portati verso il baratro. Sì: li hai portati lì. Eppure puoi ancora sorridere, proprio come stai facendo ora. E c’è dell’altro ancora. So che tu e Harry siete inseparabili. Sicuramente, per questo motivo, se non per altro, non avresti dovuto usare il nome di sua sorella in modo così spregevole, ”  
“Stai attento, Basil. Vai troppo oltre.”
“I must parlare, e tu devi ascoltare. Devi assolutamente ascoltare. Quando hai conosciuto Lady Gwendolen, non c’era ombra di scandalo su di lei. Esiste ancora una donna perbene a [[London|Londra]] che oserebbe passeggiare con lei nel parco? Anche i suoi figli non le sono permessi di vivere con lei. Ci sono altre storie. Storie secondo cui ti si vede uscire all’[[Dawn|'alba]] da case orribili e nasconderti sotto mentite spoglie nelle peggiori bettole di [[London|Londra]]. Sono vere? Possono essere vere? Quando le ho sentite per la prima volta, ho riso. Ora, invece, mi fanno rabbrividire. E poi c’è la tua famiglia. La vita che conduci lì. Dorian, non sai cosa si dice di te. Non ti dico che non voglio predicarti. Ricordo che Harry disse una volta che tutti quelli che si trasformano in “curati dilettanti” iniziano sempre così, per poi rompere la loro parola. Voglio davvero predicarti. Voglio che tu conduca una vita tale da far rispettare te stesso dal mondo intero. Voglio che tu abbia un nome pulito e una reputazione onesta. Voglio che ti liberi di quelle persone orribili con cui ti frequenti. Non alzare le spalle in quel modo. Non essere così indifferente. Hai un grande potere. Che sia usato per il bene, non per il male. Si dice che corrompi chiunque entri in intimità con te. E che basti il tuo ingresso in una casa perché qualcosa di vergognoso ne derivi. Non so se sia vero. Come potrei saperlo? Ma si dice così di te. Mi vengono raccontate cose che sembrano impossibili da [[Doubt|dubitare]]. Lord [[Gloucester]] era uno dei miei migliori amici a [[Oxford]]. Mi mostrò una lettera scritta da sua moglie prima di morire, [[Alone|da sola]] nella sua villa a Mentone. Il tuo nome era menzionato in quella confessione terribile che ho mai letto. Gli dissi che era assurdo. Che ti conoscevo bene e che non eri capace di una cosa del genere. Ti conosco? [[Wonder|Mi chiedo se ti conosca davvero,]] Prima di poter rispondere, dovrei vedere la tua [[Soul|'anima]], ”  
“Vedere la mia [[Soul|'anima]]!” mormorò [[Dorian Gray]], alzandosi dal divano e impallidendo per il [[Fear|terrore]].  
“Sì,” rispose Hallward con gravità, nella sua voce c’era un profondo dolore, “vedere la tua [[Soul|'anima]]. Ma solo Dio può farlo, ”  
Un’amara risata di derisione sfuggì dalle labbra del giovane. “La vedrai tu stesso, stasera!” gridò, afferrando una lampada dal tavolo. “Vieni. È opera tua. Perché non dovresti guardarla? Puoi raccontare tutto al mondo dopo, se vuoi. Nessuno ti crederà. Anche se ci credessero, mi apprezzerebbero ancora di più. Conosco meglio di te l’età che hai. Nonostante tu ne parli in modo così noioso. Vieni. Ne hai parlato abbastanza della corruzione. Ora devi affrontarla faccia a faccia, ”
C'era la [[Madness|follia]] della [[Pride|orgoglio]] in ogni parola che pronunciava. Batteva il piede a terra con quel suo modo insolente da ragazzo; provava una gioia terribile all'idea che qualcun altro avrebbe condiviso il suo segreto, e che l'uomo che aveva dipinto quel ritratto, fonte di tutta la sua vergogna, avrebbe dovuto portare per il resto della vita il terribile [[Memory|ricordo]] di ciò che aveva fatto.  
“Sì,” continuò, avvicinandosi a lui e guardandolo negli occhi severi, “ti mostrerò la mia [[Soul|'anima]]. Vedrai quella cosa che pensi possa essere vista solo da Dio.”  
Hallward indietreggiò. “È blasfemia, Dorian!” esclamò. “Non devi dire cose del genere. Sono orribili e non significano nulla.”  
“Tu lo credi davvero?” rise di nuovo.  
“Lo so con certezza. Quanto a ciò che ti ho detto quella [[Night|notte]], l’ho fatto per il tuo bene. Sai che sono sempre stato un amico leale per te.”  
“Non toccarmi. Finisci quello che hai da dire.”
Un lampo di [[Pain|dolore]] attraversò il viso del pittore. Si fermò per un momento, e provò un forte sentimento di compassione. Dopotutto, che diritto aveva di intromettersi nella vita di [[Dorian Gray]]? Se avesse fatto anche solo la metà di ciò di cui si diceva su di lui, quante sofferenze doveva aver provato! Poi si raddrizzò e andò vicino al camino, rimanendo lì a guardare i tronchi che bruciavano, con le loro ceneri simili alla brina e il fuoco che pulsava al loro interno.  
“Sto aspettando, Basil,” disse il giovane con voce ferma e chiara.  
Lui si girò. “Quello che devo dire è questo,” esclamò. “Devi darmi una spiegazione per queste orribili accuse rivolte contro di te. Se mi dici che sono completamente false, da capo a fondo, ti crederò. Negale, Dorian. Non vedi cosa sto passando? Mio Dio, non dirmi che sei cattivo, corrotto e vergognoso.”  
[[Dorian Gray]] sorrise. Le sue labbra si incurvarono in un sorriso di disprezzo. “Vieni su, Basil,” disse tranquillamente. “Tenho un diario nel quale registro ogni giorno della mia vita, e non lascia mai la stanza in cui viene scritto. Te lo mostrerò se vieni con me.”
“Verrò con te, Dorian, se lo desideri. Vedo che ho perso il treno. Non importa, posso andare domani. Ma non chiedermi di leggere nulla stasera. Tutto ciò che voglio è una risposta semplice alla mia domanda.”  
“Ti verrà data la risposta di sopra. Non potevo dartela qui. Non dovrai leggere a lungo.”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_14" data-title="The Picture of Dorian Gray — Chapter 13" data-chapter="Chapter 14" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="archetype/artist,motif/blood,motif/clock,motif/dust,motif/fire,motif/grave,motif/leaves,motif/night,motif/pain,motif/poison,motif/prayer,motif/snow,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,motif/wind,motif/window,concept/beauty,concept/despair,concept/grotesque,concept/inner_life,concept/madness,concept/pride,concept/temptation,concept/wonder,form/parody,form/satire,setting/paris,character/basil_hallward,character/christ,character/dorian_gray"></span>


CHAPTER 13
He passed out of the room and began the ascent, [[Basil Hallward]] following close behind. They walked softly, as men do instinctively at [[Night|night]]. The lamp cast fantastic shadows on the wall and staircase. A rising [[Wind|wind]] made some of the windows rattle.
When they reached the top landing, Dorian set the lamp down on the floor, and taking out the key, turned it in the lock. “You insist on knowing, Basil?” he asked in a low voice.
“Yes.”
“I am delighted,” he answered, smiling. Then he added, somewhat harshly, “You are the one man in the world who is entitled to know everything about me. You have had more to do with my life than you think”; and, taking up the lamp, he opened the door and went in. A cold current of air passed them, and the light shot up for a moment in a flame of murky orange. He shuddered. “Shut the door behind you,” he whispered, as he placed the lamp on the table.
Hallward glanced round him with a puzzled expression. The room looked as if it had not been lived in for years. A faded Flemish tapestry, a curtained picture, an old Italian cassone, and an almost empty book-case — that was all that it seemed to contain, besides a chair and a table. As [[Dorian Gray]] was lighting a half-burned candle that was standing on the mantelshelf, he saw that the whole place was covered with [[Dust|dust]] and that the carpet was in holes. A mouse ran scuffling behind the wainscoting. There was a damp odour of mildew.
“So you think that it is only God who sees the [[Soul|soul]], Basil? Draw that curtain back, and you will see mine.”
The voice that spoke was cold and cruel. “You are mad, Dorian, or playing a part,” muttered Hallward, frowning.
“You won’t? Then I must do it myself,” said the young man, and he tore the curtain from its rod and flung it on the ground.
An exclamation of horror broke from the painter’s lips as he saw in the dim light the hideous face on the canvas grinning at him. There was something in its expression that filled him with disgust and loathing. Good heavens! it was [[Dorian Gray]]’s own face that he was looking at! The horror, whatever it was, had not yet entirely spoiled that marvellous [[Beauty|beauty]]. There was still some gold in the thinning hair and some scarlet on the sensual mouth. The sodden eyes had kept something of the loveliness of their blue, the noble curves had not yet completely passed away from chiselled nostrils and from plastic throat. Yes, it was Dorian himself. But who had done it? He seemed to recognize his own brushwork, and the frame was his own design. The idea was monstrous, yet he felt afraid. He seized the lighted candle, and held it to the picture. In the left-hand corner was his own name, traced in long letters of bright vermilion.
It was some foul [[Parody|parody]], some infamous ignoble [[Satire|satire]]. He had never done that. Still, it was his own picture. He knew it, and he felt as if his [[Blood|blood]] had changed in a moment from [[Fire|fire]] to sluggish ice. His own picture! What did it mean? Why had it altered? He turned and looked at [[Dorian Gray]] with the eyes of a sick man. His mouth twitched, and his parched tongue seemed unable to articulate. He passed his hand across his forehead. It was dank with clammy sweat.
The young man was leaning against the mantelshelf, watching him with that strange expression that one sees on the faces of those who are absorbed in a play when some great [[artist]] is acting. There was neither real sorrow in it nor real joy. There was simply the passion of the spectator, with perhaps a flicker of triumph in his eyes. He had taken the flower out of his coat, and was smelling it, or pretending to do so.
“What does this mean?” cried Hallward, at last. His own voice sounded shrill and curious in his ears.
“Years ago, when I was a boy,” said [[Dorian Gray]], crushing the flower in his hand, “you met me, flattered me, and taught me to be vain of my good looks. One day you introduced me to a friend of yours, who explained to me the [[Wonder|wonder]] of youth, and you finished a portrait of me that revealed to me the [[Wonder|wonder]] of [[Beauty|beauty]]. In a mad moment that, even now, I don’t know whether I regret or not, I made a wish, perhaps you would call it a [[prayer]]....”
“I remember it! Oh, how [[Well|well]] I remember it! No! the thing is impossible. The room is damp. Mildew has got into the canvas. The paints I used had some wretched mineral [[Poison|poison]] in them. I tell you the thing is impossible.”
“Ah, what is impossible?” murmured the young man, going over to the [[Window|window]] and leaning his forehead against the cold, mist-stained glass.
“You told me you had destroyed it.”
“I was wrong. It has destroyed me.”
“I don’t believe it is my picture.”
“Can’t you see your ideal in it?” said Dorian bitterly.
“My ideal, as you call it...”
“As you called it.”
“There was nothing evil in it, nothing shameful. You were to me such an ideal as I shall never meet again. This is the face of a satyr.”
“It is the face of my [[Soul|soul]].”
“[[Christ]]! what a thing I must have worshipped! It has the eyes of a devil.”
“Each of us has heaven and hell in him, Basil,” cried Dorian with a wild gesture of [[Despair|despair]].
Hallward turned again to the portrait and gazed at it. “My God! If it is true,” he exclaimed, “and this is what you have done with your life, why, you must be worse even than those who talk against you fancy you to be!” He held the light up again to the canvas and examined it. The surface seemed to be quite undisturbed and as he had left it. It was from within, apparently, that the foulness and horror had come. Through some strange quickening of [[Inner Life|inner life]] the leprosies of sin were slowly eating the thing away. The rotting of a corpse in a watery [[Grave|grave]] was not so fearful.
His hand shook, and the candle fell from its socket on the floor and lay there sputtering. He placed his foot on it and put it out. Then he flung himself into the rickety chair that was standing by the table and buried his face in his hands.
“Good God, Dorian, what a lesson! What an awful lesson!” There was no answer, but he could hear the young man sobbing at the [[Window|window]]. “Pray, Dorian, pray,” he murmured. “What is it that one was taught to say in one’s boyhood? ‘Lead us not into [[Temptation|temptation]]. Forgive us our sins. Wash away our iniquities.’ Let us say that together. The [[prayer]] of your [[Pride|pride]] has been answered. The [[prayer]] of your repentance will be answered also. I worshipped you too much. I am punished for it. You worshipped yourself too much. We are both punished.”
[[Dorian Gray]] turned slowly around and looked at him with tear-dimmed eyes. “It is too late, Basil,” he faltered.
“It is never too late, Dorian. Let us kneel down and try if we cannot remember a [[prayer]]. Isn’t there a verse somewhere, ‘Though your sins be as scarlet, yet I will make them as white as [[Snow|snow]]’?”
“Those words mean nothing to me now.”
“Hush! Don’t say that. You have done enough evil in your life. My God! Don’t you see that accursed thing leering at us?”
[[Dorian Gray]] glanced at the picture, and suddenly an uncontrollable feeling of hatred for [[Basil Hallward]] came over him, as though it had been suggested to him by the image on the canvas, whispered into his ear by those grinning lips. The mad passions of a hunted animal stirred within him, and he loathed the man who was seated at the table, more than in his whole life he had ever loathed anything. He glanced wildly around. Something glimmered on the top of the painted chest that faced him. His eye fell on it. He knew what it was. It was a knife that he had brought up, some days before, to cut a piece of cord, and had forgotten to take away with him. He moved slowly towards it, passing Hallward as he did so. As soon as he got behind him, he seized it and turned round. Hallward stirred in his chair as if he was going to rise. He rushed at him and dug the knife into the great vein that is behind the ear, crushing the man’s head down on the table and stabbing again and again.
There was a stifled groan and the horrible sound of some one choking with [[Blood|blood]]. Three times the outstretched arms shot up convulsively, waving [[Grotesque|grotesque]], stiff-fingered hands in the air. He stabbed him twice more, but the man did not move. Something began to trickle on the floor. He waited for a moment, still pressing the head down. Then he threw the knife on the table, and listened.
He could hear nothing, but the drip, drip on the threadbare carpet. He opened the door and went out on the landing. The [[house]] was absolutely quiet. No one was about. For a few seconds he stood bending over the balustrade and peering down into the black seething [[Well|well]] of darkness. Then he took out the key and returned to the room, locking himself in as he did so.
The thing was still seated in the chair, straining over the table with bowed head, and humped back, and long fantastic arms. Had it not been for the red jagged tear in the neck and the clotted black pool that was slowly widening on the table, one would have said that the man was simply asleep.
How quickly it had all been done! He felt strangely calm, and walking over to the [[Window|window]], opened it and stepped out on the balcony. The [[Wind|wind]] had blown the fog away, and the sky was like a monstrous peacock’s tail, starred with myriads of golden eyes. He looked down and saw the policeman going his rounds and flashing the long beam of his lantern on the doors of the silent houses. The crimson spot of a prowling hansom gleamed at the corner and then vanished. A woman in a fluttering shawl was creeping slowly by the railings, staggering as she went. Now and then she stopped and peered back. Once, she began to sing in a hoarse voice. The policeman strolled over and said something to her. She stumbled away, laughing. A bitter blast swept across the square. The gas-lamps flickered and became blue, and the leafless trees shook their black iron branches to and fro. He shivered and went back, closing the [[Window|window]] behind him.
Having reached the door, he turned the key and opened it. He did not even glance at the murdered man. He felt that the secret of the whole thing was not to realize the situation. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait to which all his misery had been due had gone out of his life. That was enough.
Then he remembered the lamp. It was a rather curious one of Moorish workmanship, made of dull silver inlaid with arabesques of burnished steel, and studded with coarse turquoises. Perhaps it might be missed by his servant, and questions would be asked. He hesitated for a moment, then he turned back and took it from the table. He could not help seeing the dead thing. How still it was! How horribly white the long hands looked! It was like a dreadful wax image.
Having locked the door behind him, he crept quietly downstairs. The woodwork creaked and seemed to cry out as if in [[Pain|pain]]. He stopped several times and waited. No: everything was still. It was merely the sound of his own footsteps.
When he reached the library, he saw the bag and coat in the corner. They must be hidden away somewhere. He unlocked a secret press that was in the wainscoting, a press in which he kept his own curious disguises, and put them into it. He could easily burn them afterwards. Then he pulled out his watch. It was twenty minutes to two.
He sat down and began to think. Every year — every month, almost — men were strangled in England for what he had done. There had been a [[Madness|madness]] of murder in the air. Some red star had come too close to the earth.... And yet, what evidence was there against him? [[Basil Hallward]] had left the [[house]] at eleven. No one had seen him come in again. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed.... [[Paris]]! Yes. It was to [[Paris]] that Basil had gone, and by the midnight train, as he had intended. With his curious reserved habits, it would be months before any suspicions would be roused. Months! Everything could be destroyed long before then.
A sudden thought struck him. He put on his fur coat and hat and went out into the hall. There he paused, hearing the slow heavy tread of the policeman on the pavement outside and seeing the flash of the bull’s-eye reflected in the [[Window|window]]. He waited and held his breath.
After a few moments he drew back the latch and slipped out, shutting the door very gently behind him. Then he began ringing the bell. In about five minutes his valet appeared, half-dressed and looking very drowsy.
“I am sorry to have had to wake you up, Francis,” he said, stepping in; “but I had forgotten my latch-key. What [[Time|time]] is it?”
“Ten minutes past two, sir,” answered the man, looking at the [[Clock|clock]] and blinking.
“Ten minutes past two? How horribly late! You must wake me at nine to-morrow. I have some work to do.”
“All right, sir.”
“Did any one call this evening?”
“Mr. Hallward, sir. He stayed here till eleven, and then he went away to catch his train.”
“Oh! I am sorry I didn’t see him. Did he leave any message?”
“No, sir, except that he would write to you from [[Paris]], if he did not find you at the club.”
“That will do, Francis. Don’t forget to call me at nine to-morrow.”
“No, sir.”
The man shambled down the passage in his slippers.
[[Dorian Gray]] threw his hat and coat upon the table and passed into the library. For a quarter of an hour he walked up and down the room, biting his lip and thinking. Then he took down the Blue Book from one of the shelves and began to turn over the [[Leaves|leaves]]. “Alan Campbell, 152, Hertford Street, Mayfair.” Yes; that was the man he wanted.

**CAPITOLO 13**  
Uscì dalla stanza e iniziò a salire le scale; [[Basil Hallward]] lo seguiva da vicino. Camminavano in silenzio, come fanno istintivamente gli uomini di notte. La lampada proiettava ombre strane sul muro e sulla scala; un vento crescente faceva tremare alcune finestre.  
Quando raggiunsero il piano superiore, Dorian posò la lampada a terra, prese la chiave e la infilò nella serratura. “Insisti davvero a saperlo, Basil?” chiese a bassa voce.  
“Sì.”  
“Ne sono felice,” rispose lui sorridendo. Poi aggiunse, con tono un po’ severo: “Sei l’unica persona al mondo che ha il diritto di sapere tutto su di me. Hai avuto un ruolo più importante nella mia vita di quanto tu possa immaginare, ” Prese la lampada e aprì la porta; una corrente d’aria fredda li investì, e la luce si accese per un istante in un bagliore arancione scuro. Dorian rabbrividì. “Chiudi la porta dietro di te,” sussurrò, posando la lampada sul tavolo.  
Hallward guardò intorno con espressione perplessa. La stanza sembrava non essere stata abitata da anni: un tappeto fiammingo sbiadito, un quadro coperto da una tenda, un vecchio armadio italiano e uno scaffale quasi vuoto. Non c’era molto, a parte una sedia e un tavolo. Mentre [[Dorian Gray]] accendeva una candela mezza consumata sul camino, notò che tutto era coperto di polvere e che il tappeto presentava dei buchi; un topo correva dietro la cornice del muro. C’era anche un odore umido di muffa.  
“Quindi pensi che solo Dio possa vedere l’anima, Basil? Tira indietro quella tenda e vedrai la mia, ”  
La voce era fredda e crudele. “Sei pazzo, Dorian, o stai recitando una parte,” mormorò Hallward, corrugando la fronte.  
“Non vuoi farlo? Allora dovrò farlo da solo, ” disse il giovane, strappando la tenda dalla sua barra e gettandola a terra.  
Un grido di orrore sfuggì dalle labbra del pittore: nella penombra, vide sul quadro il volto orribile di [[Dorian Gray]] che gli sorrideva. C’era qualcosa nel suo sguardo che lo riempì di disgusto e odio. Per Dio, era proprio il viso di Dorian! L’orrore, però, non aveva ancora completamente distrutto quella meravigliosa [[Beauty|bellezza]]: i capelli radi conservavano ancora un tocco d’oro, le labbra sensuali un colore rosso scarlatto. Gli occhi umidi mantenevano ancora il loro colore azzurro. Sì, era proprio Dorian. Ma chi aveva fatto tutto ciò? Sembrava riconoscere la propria mano nell’esecuzione dei dettagli. E il quadro stesso era stato realizzato secondo i suoi disegni. L’idea era orribile, ma provava paura. Prese la candela accesa e la avvicinò al dipinto. Nell’angolo sinistro c’era scritto il suo nome, tracciato con lettere rosso vivo.
Era una qualche oscena [[Parody|parodia]], una qualche infame e ignobile [[Satire|satira]]. Lui non aveva mai fatto nulla del genere. Eppure era la sua stessa immagine. Lo sapeva, e sentiva come se il suo [[Blood|sangue]] si fosse improvvisamente trasformato da [[Fire|fuoco]] in ghiaccio vischioso. La sua stessa immagine. Cosa significava? Perché era cambiata? Si girò a guardare [[Dorian Gray]] con gli occhi di un uomo malato. Le sue labbra tremavano, e la sua lingua arsa sembrava incapace di articolare parole. Si passò una mano sulla fronte: era bagnata di sudore freddo e appiccicoso.
Il giovane era appoggiato allo scaffale del camino, a osservarlo con quell’espressione strana che si vede sul viso di chi è completamente assorbito da un’opera teatrale quando un grande [[artist|artista]] sta recitando. Non c’era né vera tristezza né vera gioia nei suoi occhi. Solo l’entusiasmo dello spettatore, forse accompagnato da un barlume di trionfo. Aveva tolto il fiore dal proprio cappotto e lo stava annusando, o fingeva di farlo.
“Cosa significa tutto questo?” gridò finalmente Hallward. La sua stessa voce gli sembrava stridula e insolita nelle orecchie.
“Anni fa, quando ero un ragazzo,” disse [[Dorian Gray]], schiacciando il fiore nella sua mano, “mi hai conosciuto, mi hai lusingato e mi hai insegnato ad essere vanitoso della mia bellezza. Un giorno mi hai presentato un tuo amico, che mi ha spiegato la [[Wonder|magnificenza]] della giovinezza; inoltre, hai completato il mio ritratto, rivelandomi la [[Wonder|misteriosità]] della [[Beauty|bellezza]]. In un momento di follia, che, anche ora, non so se rimpianga o meno, ho fatto un desiderio, forse potresti chiamarlo una [[prayer|preghiera]], ”  
“Me lo ricordo! Oh, quanto me lo ricordo bene! No, è impossibile. La stanza è umida; il telaio del ritratto è infestato di muffa. I colori che ho usato contenevano qualche orribile sostanza minerale velenosa. Te lo dico: è impossibile.”  
“Ah, cosa può essere considerato impossibile?” mormorò il giovane, avvicinandosi alla [[Window|finestra]] e appoggiando la fronte al vetro freddo e offuscato dalla nebbia.  
“Mi hai detto di aver distrutto quel ritratto, ”  
“Mi sbagliavo. È stato quel ritratto a distruggermi.”  
“Non credo che si tratti del mio dipinto, ”  
“Non riesci forse a vedere il tuo ideale in esso?” disse Dorian con amarezza.  
“Il mio ideale, come lo chiami tu, ”  
“Come lo hai chiamato tu, ”
“Non c’era nulla di malvagio in tutto ciò, nulla di vergognoso. Tu eri per me un ideale che non incontrerò mai più. Questo è il volto di un satiro.”  
“È il volto della mia [[Soul|'anima]].”  
“[[Christ|Cristo]]! Quanto devo aver adorato questa cosa. Ha gli occhi di un demone.”  
“Ognuno di noi porta in sé il cielo e l’inferno, Basil,” gridò Dorian con un gesto disperato.
Hallward si voltò di nuovo verso il ritratto e lo fissò. “Mio Dio! Se è vero, ”, esclamò, “se davvero questo è ciò che hai fatto della tua vita, allora devi essere ancora peggiore di quanto coloro che parlano contro di te possano immaginare!” Sollevò di nuovo la candela verso la tela e l’esaminò attentamente. La superficie sembrava del tutto intatta, esattamente come l’aveva lasciata. Era chiaramente dall’interno che provenivano quella corruzione e quell’orrore: attraverso qualche strana intensificazione della sua [[Inner Life|vita interiore]], le “lebbra” del peccato stavano lentamente distruggendo quel ritratto. Il marcire di un cadavere in una tomba piena d’acqua non era nemmeno paragonabile a questa scena orribile.  
La sua mano tremò; la candela cadde dal supporto e si spense sul pavimento. Lui la schiacciò con il piede, poi si lasciò cadere sulla sedia traballante accanto al tavolo e nascose il viso tra le mani.
“Dio mio, Dorian, che lezione. Che terribile lezione!” Non ci fu risposta, ma si poteva sentire il giovane singhiozzare alla [[Window|finestra]]. “Prega, Dorian, prega, ” mormorò. “Che cosa si insegna a dire nell’infanzia? ‘Non indurci nella tentazione. Perdona i nostri peccati. Lavaci dai nostri misfatti.’ Diciamolo insieme. La [[prayer|preghiera]] della tua [[Pride|orgoglio]] è stata ascoltata. Anche la preghiera del tuo pentimento verrà ascoltata. Ti ho adorato troppo. Ne pago le conseguenze. E tu hai adorato te stesso troppo. Entrambi ne paghiamo le conseguenze.”  
[[Dorian Gray]] si girò lentamente, guardandolo con occhi pieni di lacrime. “È troppo tardi, Basil, ” mormorò.  
“Non è mai troppo tardi, Dorian. Mettiamoci in ginocchio e proviamo a ricordare una preghiera. Non c’è forse un versetto che dice: ‘Anche se i tuoi peccati sono rossi come il sangue, io li renderò bianchi come la neve’?”  
“Quei parole ormai non significano nulla per me, ”  
“Taci. Non dire così. Hai commesso abbastanza male nella tua vita. Mio Dio. Non vedi quella cosa maledetta che ci sta fissando?”
[[Dorian Gray]] gettò un’occhiata al dipinto, e all’improvviso provò un sentimento incontrollabile di odio per [[Basil Hallward]], come se quell’immagine sulla tela glielo avesse suggerito, come se quelle labbra sorridenti glielo avessero sussurrato all’orecchio. Le folli passioni di un animale braccato si risvegliarono in lui; odiava quell’uomo seduto al tavolo più di quanto avesse mai odiato qualcosa in tutta la sua vita. Guardò intorno disperatamente. Qualcosa brillava sul cassetto dipinto di fronte a lui. I suoi occhi lo individuarono: era un coltello che aveva portato lì alcuni giorni prima per tagliare un pezzo di corda, ma se n’era dimenticato di prendere con sé. Si avvicinò lentamente, passando accanto a Hallward; non appena gli fu alle spalle, lo afferrò e si girò di scatto. Hallward si mosse sulla sedia, come se stesse per alzarsi. Lui gli si gettò addosso e conficcò il coltello nella vena grande dietro l’orecchio, schiacciandogli la testa contro il tavolo e pugnalando ancora e ancora.
Si udì un gemito soffocato e il terribile suono di qualcuno che stava soffocando nel [[Blood|sangue]]. Tre volte le braccia tese si alzarono convulsivamente, agitando mani grottesche e rigide nell’aria. Lui lo pugnalò altre due volte, ma l’uomo non si mosse. Qualcosa iniziò a gocciolare sul pavimento. Aspettò un momento, continuando a premere la testa a terra; poi gettò il coltello sul tavolo e ascoltò. Non sentiva nulla, solo quel gocciolio sul tappeto logoro. Aprì la porta e uscì sul corridoio: la [[house|casa]] era completamente silenziosa. Nessuno c’era. Per qualche secondo rimase in piedi, appoggiato alla balaustra, a guardare giù nel buio profondo di quella oscura “prigione”. Poi prese la chiave e tornò nella stanza, chiudendosi dentro a chiave.  
Quell’uomo era ancora seduto sulla sedia, curvo sopra il tavolo con la testa bassa. Se non fosse stato per quella ferita rossa e irregolare sul collo e per quel lago di sangue nero che si stava lentamente allargando sul tavolo, si sarebbe potuto pensare che quell’uomo stesse semplicemente dormendo.  
Com’era tutto accaduto così in fretta. Si sentiva stranamente calmo. Andò alla [[Window|finestra]], la aprì e uscì sul balcone. Il [[Wind|vento]] aveva spazzato via la nebbia; il cielo sembrava la coda di un enorme pavone, punteggiato da migliaia di stelle dorate. Guardò giù e vide il poliziotto che faceva il suo giro, illuminando con il faro le porte delle case silenziose. Un fiocco rosso di una vettura a noleggio lampeggiò all’angolo, poi scomparve. Una donna, avvolta in uno scialle fluttuante, si muoveva lentamente lungo la ringhiera, barcollando. Di tanto in tanto si fermava e guardava indietro; una volta iniziò a cantare con voce rauca. Il poliziotto le si avvicinò e le disse qualcosa; lei si allontanò ridendo. Un soffio gelido attraversò la piazza; i lampioni a gas tremolarono e diventarono blu; gli alberi spogli scossero le loro braccia nere. Rabbrividì e tornò dentro, chiudendo la [[Window|finestra]] dietro di sé.  
Arrivato alla porta, girò la chiave e l’aprì. Non guardò nemmeno il cadavere dell’uomo assassinato. Sentiva che il segreto di tutto ciò non stava nel rendersi conto della realtà. Quel “amico” che aveva dipinto quel ritratto fatale, responsabile di tutta la sua sofferenza, era ormai scomparso dalla sua vita. E questo era sufficiente.
Poi si ricordò della lampada. Era una lampada piuttosto curiosa, realizzata in argento opaco con arabeschi in acciaio lucido e incastonata di turchesi grezzi. Forse il suo servitore se ne sarebbe accorto e avrebbero iniziato a fare domande. Esitò per un momento, poi tornò indietro e la prese dal tavolo. Non poté fare a meno di guardare quel cadavere. Quanto era immobile. Quanto erano pallide quelle lunghe mani. Sembrava una terribile statua di cera.
Dopo aver chiuso la porta alle sue spalle, scese silenziosamente le scale. I legni scricchiolavano, come se provassero dolore. Si fermò più volte, aspettando. No: tutto era tranquillo; era soltanto il suono dei suoi passi.  
Quando arrivò in biblioteca, vide la borsa e il cappotto nell’angolo. Dovevano essere nascosti da qualche parte. Aprì una cassaforte segreta nascosta nel rivestimento della parete, dove teneva i propri travestimenti curiosi, e li mise lì dentro. Poteva bruciarli facilmente in seguito. Poi tirò fuori l’orologio: mancavano venti minuti alle due.
Si sedette e iniziò a riflettere. Ogni anno – quasi ogni mese – in Inghilterra uomini venivano strangolati per ciò che lui aveva fatto. C’era stata un’ondata di omicidi. Qualche “stella rossa” doveva essersi avvicinata troppo alla Terra. Eppure, quali prove c’erano contro di lui? [[Basil Hallward]] era uscito di casa alle undici; nessuno lo aveva visto rientrare. La maggior parte dei domestici si trovava a Selby Royal; il suo valletto era andato a letto. [[Paris|Parigi]]! Sì, Basil era partito per [[Paris|Parigi]], con il treno di mezzanotte, come aveva previsto. Con le sue abitudini riservate e curiose, sarebbero trascorsi mesi prima che qualcuno iniziasse a sospettare. Mesi! Tutto poteva essere distrutto molto prima di allora.  
Un’idea improvvisa gli balenò in mente. Indossò il cappotto di pelliccia e il cappello, poi uscì nel corridoio. Lì si fermò: sentiva i passi lenti e pesanti del poliziotto sul marciapiede esterno, e vide il bagliore della torcia riflettersi nella finestra. Aspettò, trattenendo il respiro. Dopo alcuni istanti aprì la porta e uscì silenziosamente, richiudendola con delicatezza alle sue spalle. Poi iniziò a suonare il campanello. Dopo circa cinque minuti, il suo valletto apparve, ancora mezzo vestito e sembrava molto assonnato.
“Mi dispiace di aver dovuto svegliarti, Francis,” disse entrando nella stanza; “ma avevo dimenticato la mia chiave. Che ora è?”  
“Sono le dieci e venti, signore,” rispose l’uomo, guardando l’orologio e battendo le palpebre.  
“Le dieci e venti? Che orrore. Devi svegliarmi alle nove di domani; ho del lavoro da fare.”  
“Va bene, signore.”  
“Qualcuno ha chiamato stasera?”  
“Il signor Hallward, signore. È rimasto qui fino all’undici, poi è andato a prendere il treno.”  
“Oh. Mi dispiace di non averlo incontrato. Ha lasciato qualche messaggio?”  
“No, signore; solo che vi avrebbe scritto da [[Paris|Parigi]] se non vi avesse trovato al club.”  
“Va bene, Francis. Non dimenticare di chiamarmi alle nove domani.”  
“No, signore.”  
L’uomo si allontanò barcollando nei suoi pantofole lungo il corridoio.  
[[Dorian Gray]] gettò cappello e cappotto sul tavolo e andò in biblioteca. Per un quarto d’ora camminò avanti e indietro nella stanza, mordendosi il labbro e pensando. Poi prese il “Blue Book” da uno scaffale e iniziò a sfogliarne le pagine. “Alan Campbell, 152, Hertford Street, Mayfair, ” Sì. Quell’uomo era proprio quello che cercava.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_15" data-title="The Picture of Dorian Gray — Chapter 14" data-chapter="Chapter 15" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="archetype/shadow,motif/autumn,motif/birds,motif/blood,motif/cave,motif/city,motif/clock,motif/death,motif/desire,motif/dust,motif/fire,motif/flowers,motif/garden,motif/grave,motif/home,motif/love,motif/memory,motif/night,motif/pain,motif/rose,motif/secrets,motif/silence,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,motif/window,concept/beauty,concept/body,concept/courage,concept/exile,concept/grotesque,concept/imagination,concept/melancholy,concept/pride,concept/suicide,concept/wonder,setting/oxford,setting/paris,setting/venice,character/basil_hallward,character/dorian_gray,character/lord_henry_wotton,character/venus"></span>


CHAPTER 14
At nine o’[[Clock|clock]] the next morning his servant came in with a cup of chocolate on a tray and opened the shutters. Dorian was sleeping quite peacefully, lying on his right side, with one hand underneath his cheek. He looked like a boy who had been tired out with play, or study.
The man had to touch him twice on the shoulder before he woke, and as he opened his eyes a faint smile passed across his lips, as though he had been lost in some delightful dream. Yet he had not dreamed at all. His [[Night|night]] had been untroubled by any images of pleasure or of [[Pain|pain]]. But youth smiles without any reason. It is one of its chiefest charms.
He turned round, and leaning upon his elbow, began to sip his chocolate. The mellow November sun came streaming into the room. The sky was bright, and there was a genial warmth in the air. It was almost like a morning in May.
Gradually the events of the preceding [[Night|night]] crept with silent, [[Blood|blood]]-stained feet into his brain and reconstructed themselves there with terrible distinctness. He winced at the [[Memory|memory]] of all that he had suffered, and for a moment the same curious feeling of loathing for [[Basil Hallward]] that had made him kill him as he sat in the chair came back to him, and he grew cold with passion. The dead man was still sitting there, too, and in the sunlight now. How horrible that was! Such hideous things were for the darkness, not for the day.
He felt that if he brooded on what he had gone through he would sicken or grow mad. There were sins whose fascination was more in the [[Memory|memory]] than in the doing of them, strange triumphs that gratified the [[Pride|pride]] more than the passions, and gave to the intellect a quickened sense of joy, greater than any joy they brought, or could ever bring, to the senses. But this was not one of them. It was a thing to be driven out of the mind, to be drugged with poppies, to be strangled lest it might strangle one itself.
When the half-hour struck, he passed his hand across his forehead, and then got up hastily and dressed himself with even more than his usual care, giving a good deal of attention to the choice of his necktie and scarf-pin and changing his rings more than once. He spent a long [[Time|time]] also over breakfast, tasting the various dishes, talking to his valet about some new liveries that he was thinking of getting made for the servants at Selby, and going through his correspondence. At some of the letters, he smiled. Three of them bored him. One he read several times over and then tore up with a slight look of annoyance in his face. “That awful thing, a woman’s [[Memory|memory]]!” as Lord Henry had once said.
After he had drunk his cup of black coffee, he wiped his lips slowly with a napkin, motioned to his servant to wait, and going over to the table, sat down and wrote two letters. One he put in his pocket, the other he handed to the valet.
“Take this round to 152, Hertford Street, Francis, and if Mr. Campbell is out of town, get his address.”
As soon as he was [[Alone|alone]], he lit a cigarette and began sketching upon a piece of paper, drawing first [[Flowers|flowers]] and bits of architecture, and then human faces. Suddenly he remarked that every face that he drew seemed to have a fantastic likeness to [[Basil Hallward]]. He frowned, and getting up, went over to the book-case and took out a volume at hazard. He was determined that he would not think about what had happened until it became absolutely necessary that he should do so.
When he had stretched himself on the sofa, he looked at the title-page of the book. It was Gautier’s Emaux et Camees, Charpentier’s Japanese-paper edition, with the Jacquemart etching. The binding was of citron-green leather, with a design of gilt trellis-work and dotted pomegranates. It had been given to him by Adrian Singleton. As he turned over the pages, his eye fell on the poem about the hand of Lacenaire, the cold yellow hand “du supplice encore mal lavee,” with its downy red hairs and its “doigts de faune.” He glanced at his own white taper fingers, shuddering slightly in spite of himself, and passed on, till he came to those lovely stanzas upon [[Venice]]:
Sur une gamme chromatique,
    Le sein de peries ruisselant,
La [[Venus]] de l’Adriatique
    Sort de l’eau son corps [[Rose|rose]] et blanc.
Les domes, sur l’azur des ondes
    Suivant la phrase au pur contour,
S’enflent comme des gorges rondes
    Que souleve un soupir d’amour.
L’esquif aborde et me depose,
    Jetant son amarre au pilier,
Devant une facade [[Rose|rose]],
    Sur le marbre d’un escalier.
How exquisite they were! As one read them, one seemed to be floating down the green [[Water|water]]-ways of the pink and pearl [[City|city]], seated in a black gondola with silver prow and trailing curtains. The mere lines looked to him like those straight lines of turquoise-blue that follow one as one pushes out to the Lido. The sudden flashes of colour reminded him of the gleam of the opal-and-iris-throated [[Birds|birds]] that flutter round the tall honeycombed Campanile, or stalk, with such stately grace, through the dim, [[Dust|dust]]-stained arcades. Leaning back with half-closed eyes, he kept saying over and over to himself:
“Devant une facade [[Rose|rose]],
    Sur le marbre d’un escalier.”
The whole of [[Venice]] was in those two lines. He remembered the [[Autumn|autumn]] that he had passed there, and a wonderful [[Love|love]] that had stirred him to mad delightful follies. There was [[Romance|romance]] in every place. But [[Venice]], like [[Oxford]], had kept the background for [[Romance|romance]], and, to the true romantic, background was everything, or almost everything. Basil had been with him part of the [[Time|time]], and had gone wild over Tintoret. Poor Basil! What a horrible way for a man to die!
He sighed, and took up the volume again, and tried to forget. He read of the swallows that fly in and out of the little cafe at Smyrna where the Hadjis sit counting their amber beads and the turbaned merchants smoke their long tasselled pipes and talk gravely to each other; he read of the Obelisk in the Place de la Concorde that weeps [[Tears|tears]] of granite in its lonely sunless [[Exile|exile]] and longs to be back by the hot, lotus-covered Nile, where there are Sphinxes, and [[Rose|rose]]-red ibises, and white vultures with gilded claws, and crocodiles with small beryl eyes that crawl over the green steaming mud; he began to brood over those verses which, drawing music from kiss-stained marble, tell of that curious statue that Gautier compares to a contralto voice, the “monstre charmant” that couches in the porphyry-room of the Louvre. But after a [[Time|time]] the book fell from his hand. He grew nervous, and a horrible fit of terror came over him. What if Alan Campbell should be out of England? Days would elapse before he could come back. Perhaps he might refuse to come. What could he do then? Every moment was of vital importance.
They had been great friends once, five years before — almost inseparable, indeed. Then the intimacy had come suddenly to an end. When they met in society now, it was only [[Dorian Gray]] who smiled: Alan Campbell never did.
He was an extremely clever young man, though he had no real appreciation of the visible arts, and whatever little sense of the [[Beauty|beauty]] of poetry he possessed he had gained entirely from Dorian. His dominant intellectual passion was for science. At Cambridge he had spent a great deal of his [[Time|time]] working in the laboratory, and had taken a good class in the Natural Science Tripos of his year. Indeed, he was still devoted to the study of chemistry, and had a laboratory of his own in which he used to shut himself up all day long, greatly to the annoyance of his mother, who had set her heart on his standing for Parliament and had a vague idea that a chemist was a person who made up prescriptions. He was an excellent musician, however, as [[Well|well]], and played both the violin and the piano better than most amateurs. In fact, it was music that had first brought him and [[Dorian Gray]] together — music and that indefinable attraction that Dorian seemed to be able to exercise whenever he wished — and, indeed, exercised often without being conscious of it. They had met at Lady Berkshire’s the [[Night|night]] that Rubinstein played there, and after that used to be always seen together at the opera and wherever good music was going on. For eighteen months their intimacy lasted. Campbell was always either at Selby Royal or in Grosvenor Square. To him, as to many others, [[Dorian Gray]] was the type of everything that is wonderful and fascinating in life. Whether or not a quarrel had taken place between them no one ever knew. But suddenly people remarked that they scarcely spoke when they met and that Campbell seemed always to go away early from any party at which [[Dorian Gray]] was present. He had changed, too — was strangely [[Melancholy|melancholy]] at times, appeared almost to dislike hearing music, and would never himself play, giving as his excuse, when he was called upon, that he was so absorbed in science that he had no [[Time|time]] left in which to practise. And this was certainly true. Every day he seemed to become more interested in biology, and his name appeared once or twice in some of the scientific reviews in connection with certain curious experiments.
This was the man [[Dorian Gray]] was waiting for. Every second he kept glancing at the [[Clock|clock]]. As the minutes went by he became horribly agitated. At last he got up and began to pace up and down the room, looking like a beautiful caged thing. He took long stealthy strides. His hands were curiously cold.
The suspense became unbearable. [[Time]] seemed to him to be crawling with feet of lead, while he by monstrous winds was being swept towards the jagged edge of some black cleft of precipice. He knew what was waiting for him there; saw it, indeed, and, shuddering, crushed with dank hands his burning lids as though he would have robbed the very brain of sight and driven the eyeballs back into their [[Cave|cave]]. It was useless. The brain had its own food on which it battened, and the [[Imagination|imagination]], made [[Grotesque|grotesque]] by terror, twisted and distorted as a living thing by [[Pain|pain]], danced like some foul puppet on a stand and grinned through moving masks. Then, suddenly, [[Time|time]] stopped for him. Yes: that blind, slow-breathing thing crawled no more, and horrible thoughts, [[Time|time]] being dead, raced nimbly on in front, and dragged a hideous future from its [[Grave|grave]], and showed it to him. He stared at it. Its very horror made him stone.
At last the door opened and his servant entered. He turned glazed eyes upon him.
“Mr. Campbell, sir,” said the man.
A sigh of relief broke from his parched lips, and the colour came back to his cheeks.
“Ask him to come in at once, Francis.” He felt that he was himself again. His mood of cowardice had passed away.
The man bowed and retired. In a few moments, Alan Campbell walked in, looking very stern and rather pale, his pallor being intensified by his coal-black hair and dark eyebrows.
“Alan! This is kind of you. I thank you for coming.”
“I had intended never to enter your [[house]] again, Gray. But you said it was a matter of life and [[Death|death]].” His voice was hard and cold. He spoke with slow deliberation. There was a look of contempt in the steady searching gaze that he turned on Dorian. He kept his hands in the pockets of his Astrakhan coat, and seemed not to have noticed the gesture with which he had been greeted.
“Yes: it is a matter of life and [[Death|death]], Alan, and to more than one person. Sit down.”
Campbell took a chair by the table, and Dorian sat opposite to him. The two men’s eyes met. In Dorian’s there was infinite pity. He knew that what he was going to do was dreadful.
After a strained moment of [[Silence|silence]], he leaned across and said, very quietly, but watching the effect of each word upon the face of him he had sent for, “Alan, in a locked room at the top of this [[house]], a room to which nobody but myself has access, a dead man is seated at a table. He has been dead ten hours now. Don’t stir, and don’t look at me like that. Who the man is, why he died, how he died, are matters that do not concern you. What you have to do is this— “
“Stop, Gray. I don’t want to know anything further. Whether what you have told me is true or not true doesn’t concern me. I entirely decline to be mixed up in your life. Keep your horrible [[Secrets|secrets]] to yourself. They don’t interest me any more.”
“Alan, they will have to interest you. This one will have to interest you. I am awfully sorry for you, Alan. But I can’t help myself. You are the one man who is able to save me. I am forced to bring you into the matter. I have no option. Alan, you are scientific. You know about chemistry and things of that kind. You have made experiments. What you have got to do is to destroy the thing that is upstairs — to destroy it so that not a vestige of it will be left. Nobody saw this person come into the [[house]]. Indeed, at the present moment he is supposed to be in [[Paris]]. He will not be missed for months. When he is missed, there must be no trace of him found here. You, Alan, you must change him, and everything that belongs to him, into a handful of ashes that I may scatter in the air.”
“You are mad, Dorian.”
“Ah! I was waiting for you to call me Dorian.”
“You are mad, I tell you — mad to imagine that I would raise a finger to help you, mad to make this monstrous confession. I will have nothing to do with this matter, whatever it is. Do you think I am going to peril my reputation for you? What is it to me what devil’s work you are up to?”
“It was [[suicide]], Alan.”
“I am glad of that. But who drove him to it? You, I should fancy.”
“Do you still refuse to do this for me?”
“Of course I refuse. I will have absolutely nothing to do with it. I don’t care what shame comes on you. You deserve it all. I should not be sorry to see you disgraced, publicly disgraced. How dare you ask me, of all men in the world, to mix myself up in this horror? I should have thought you knew more about people’s characters. Your friend [[Lord Henry Wotton]] can’t have taught you much about psychology, whatever else he has taught you. Nothing will induce me to stir a step to help you. You have come to the wrong man. Go to some of your friends. Don’t come to me.”
“Alan, it was murder. I killed him. You don’t know what he had made me suffer. Whatever my life is, he had more to do with the making or the marring of it than poor Harry has had. He may not have intended it, the result was the same.”
“Murder! Good God, Dorian, is that what you have come to? I shall not inform upon you. It is not my business. Besides, without my stirring in the matter, you are certain to be arrested. Nobody ever commits a crime without doing something stupid. But I will have nothing to do with it.”
